verses.text: Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? are not ye my work in the Lord?
If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord.
Mine answer to them that do examine me is this,
Have we not power to eat and to drink?
Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas?
Or I only and Barnabas, have not we power to forbear working?
Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges? who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof? or who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock?
Say I these things as a man? or saith not the law the same also?
For it is written in the law of Moses, Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Doth God take care for oxen?
Or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written: that he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope.
If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?
If others be partakers of this power over you, are not we rather? Nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ.
Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?
Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
But I have used none of these things: neither have I written these things, that it should be so done unto me: for it were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void.
For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward: but if against my will, a dispensation of the gospel is committed unto me.
What is my reward then? Verily that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel.
For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more.
And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law;
To them that are without law, as without law, ( being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,) that I might gain them that are without law.
To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.
And this I do for the gospel’s sake, that I might be partaker thereof with you.
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air:
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.

summary: Having just told the Corinthians that he would eat no flesh forever rather than wound a weak brother, Paul now turns the argument on himself and makes his own life the demonstration. He opens with four questions fired off in a row — "Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? are not ye my work in the Lord?" — and tells them that whatever others may say, "the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord." "Mine answer to them that do examine me is this," he says, and then, instead of defending his rights, he catalogues them at length so that laying them down will cost something visible. Has he not "power to eat and to drink"? "power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas"? Are he and Barnabas alone required to keep working with their hands? He argues from ordinary life — "Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges? who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof? or who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock?" — then from the law of Moses, "Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn," pressing the question "Doth God take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes?" and answering that "he that ploweth should plow in hope." If the apostles have "sown unto you spiritual things," it is no great matter to "reap your carnal things." He argues finally from the sanctuary — "they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar" — and from the Lord's own command: "Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." Then the whole structure is renounced in a sentence: "Nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ." Preaching itself earns him nothing to boast in, "for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!" His only wage is to have no wage — "that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel." From this renunciation flows the chapter's most quoted principle: "though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more." To the Jews he became as a Jew, to those under the law as under the law, "To them that are without law, as without law, (being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,)" and "To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." The chapter closes in the stadium. "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain." Every competitor "is temperate in all things" for "a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible." So Paul runs "not as uncertainly" and fights "not as one that beateth the air," and ends with a warning aimed squarely at himself: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway."
takeaways: Paul spends fourteen verses proving a right he has no intention of using, and the length of the proof is the point. Nature says the soldier does not fund his own campaign and "who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof?"; the law says "Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn"; the sanctuary says "they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar"; and above all "the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." Only after the right is raised as high as it can go does he set it down — "Nevertheless we have not used this power." A surrender is worth nothing if the thing surrendered was never really owned, so Paul establishes ownership first and then gives it away.

The criterion that governs the renunciation is not personal preference but effect on others: he suffers all things "lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ." This is the same test he had just applied to meat offered to idols, now turned inward, and it reframes the whole question of Christian liberty. The relevant question is never merely whether an act is permitted, since Paul concedes at every step that support is permitted and even commanded, but whether insisting on the permission would put weight on the gospel that someone else has to carry. A right that becomes an obstacle to another's salvation is a right worth losing.

Preaching gives Paul no ground for pride because it was never his idea. "For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!" He distinguishes between doing the work "willingly," for which there is a reward, and doing it "against my will," in which case "a dispensation of the gospel is committed unto me" regardless — the commission holds either way, but only the free embrace of it is crowned. A calling is not an accomplishment; the most one can do with a debt is to pay it gladly, and Paul's chosen way of paying gladly is to refuse payment.

"I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" has a fixed center that the slogan usually loses. Paul bends on custom — Jewish observance among Jews, freedom from it among Gentiles, weakness among the weak — but immediately guards the boundary in the same breath: he is "without law" only in the sense of not being under the Mosaic code, "being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ." Accommodation reaches as far as culture and no further; it is a strategy for entering another person's world, not a licence to leave Christ's. And the aim is stated with sober modesty — not to win everyone but "by all means save some."

The direction of the movement is always downward. Paul is "free from all men" and makes himself "servant unto all"; he does not summon the weak to rise to his level of knowledge but goes down to theirs — "To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak." Where the Corinthians used their strength as a platform, Paul spends his on descent. The pattern is the one he has been urging on them all along: the strong exist for the weak, and knowledge is measured by whether it can stoop.

The chapter ends with an apostle warning himself. The images are athletic and unsentimental — a race in which "one receiveth the prize," a discipline in which "every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things," a fight that is not shadowboxing, "not as one that beateth the air." Paul's bodily discipline is not contempt for the body but training of it: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection." And the stated reason is the possibility of personal loss — "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway." Preaching to others is no guarantee for the preacher; the crown is "incorruptible," but it is still run for.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 25:4 — Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn
crossRefs.why: Paul lifts this single line out of a chapter of civil ordinances and asks "Doth God take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes?" The move shows how he reads the law: a humane rule about a working animal carries a principle about all who labour, so that the ox threshing with its mouth free becomes the pattern for the preacher who lives of the gospel.

crossRefs.label: Luke 10:7 — the labourer is worthy of his hire
crossRefs.why: When Paul says "the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel," this is the ordinance he means. Christ sends out the seventy with instructions to accept food and lodging from those they serve, which makes support of preachers a dominical command rather than a Pauline convenience — and makes Paul's refusal of it a free renunciation of something Christ Himself granted.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 5:17-18 — Thou shalt not muzzle the ox... The labourer is worthy of his reward
crossRefs.why: The same two texts Paul joins here reappear together as the basis for honouring "the elders that rule well... especially they who labour in the word and doctrine." The pairing shows that the argument of this chapter was not a one-off self-defence but became settled teaching on the material support of ministers, even though Paul personally declined it at Corinth.

crossRefs.label: Acts 20:33-35 — these hands have ministered unto my necessities
crossRefs.why: Paul's farewell at Miletus is the same policy stated in his own voice years later: "I have coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel," and manual labour supported both him and his companions. It confirms that "we have not used this power" describes a sustained practice, and it supplies the motive — "so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive."

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:7-9 — I have preached to you the gospel of God freely
crossRefs.why: The later letter shows the cost and the controversy of the policy defended here. Paul asks whether he "committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted," admits "I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service," and insists he was "chargeable to no man" at Corinth. Reading the two together explains why chapter 9 sounds defensive: his refusal of support was being used against him as evidence that he was no true apostle.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 3:12-14 — I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling
crossRefs.why: The runner of this chapter appears again, and again in the first person: "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after." Both passages place a mature apostle in mid-course rather than at the finish, which is why the warning about becoming "a castaway" is not false modesty but the same settled self-understanding.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the "power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas," Catholic reading grants readily that some apostles were married men, since the Gospels show Peter with a mother-in-law, and reads the verse as being about a right of support rather than about the marriage bond as such: the community owed maintenance to an apostle and to the believing woman travelling with him. On this reading the whole chapter is the charter for freely chosen renunciation in ministry. Paul possesses the right, proves it at length, and then declines it, exactly as he declines wages, so that nothing may "hinder the gospel of Christ" — and this is precisely the logic by which the Latin Church came to ask celibacy of her clergy. Celibacy is presented not as a denial that the apostles had the right, but as the disciplined embrace of the very freedom Paul models here and commends in the preceding chapter on the unmarried who care "for the things that belong to the Lord."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings take the verse as straightforward evidence that married apostles travelled with their wives at the churches' expense, and therefore as evidence against any rule that bars married men from ministry. If Peter and "the brethren of the Lord" led wives about with apostolic sanction, then the ordinary state of a minister may be marriage, and a later requirement of celibacy imposes as law what Paul here treats as one option among several. They add that Paul's own celibacy is consistently presented by him as a personal gift and a strategic freedom rather than a condition of office. Both traditions agree on the substance of what Paul is doing in the chapter: he is renouncing a genuine right, and voluntary self-denial for the gospel's sake is honourable in a way that compelled self-denial is not.

interpretationNotes.claim: The phrase "the brethren of the Lord" is understood in Catholic reading as designating a wider circle of kinsmen — cousins or other close relatives of Jesus — rather than further children of Mary. The supporting considerations offered are that the biblical vocabulary for brother regularly covers extended kinship, that the men named elsewhere as the Lord's brethren are identified as sons of another Mary, and that from the cross Jesus commits His mother to a disciple rather than to a brother, which would be strange if she had other sons. Read this way, the verse names a group of relatives who became notable missionaries in the early Church, and it leaves untouched the belief in Mary's perpetual virginity.

counterpoint.summary: Most Protestant readings take "the brethren of the Lord" in its ordinary sense as sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus, noting that the Gospels list brothers and sisters alongside His mother in a way that reads naturally as one household, and that nothing in the text signals an extended-family usage. On this view the perpetual virginity of Mary is a later development that the plain sense of passages like this one does not support and in places resists. A minority of Protestants, especially in the older confessional streams, have retained belief in Mary's perpetual virginity and read the term as Catholics do. Both traditions agree that the men in question were close relatives of Jesus, that they were not among the Twelve, and that at least one of them became a leader of the Jerusalem church.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the closing athletic passage at full weight on both halves: the crown is real and the loss is real. "So run, that ye may obtain" and "we an incorruptible" crown are read as genuine promises of reward for a life run well, and the tradition speaks of merit precisely here — not as a wage extracted from God by unaided effort, but as the reward God has freely bound Himself to give to works done in and by His grace. Correspondingly, "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" is read as a real possibility of final loss for a baptized and even apostolic man. Grace received can be forfeited by grave sin; hence the ascetical language of keeping the body under and bringing it into subjection, and hence the Church's insistence that the assurance proper to a Christian is confident hope rather than certainty of one's own final perseverance.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants are divided here, and the division is old. Those who hold to the perseverance of the saints argue that the elect cannot finally be lost and that warnings like this one are among the ordinary means by which God actually keeps them — the warning is heeded, and the heeding is itself grace; some in this stream also take "castaway" as disqualification from the race or loss of reward rather than damnation. Those who hold that grace may be finally resisted read the verse much as Catholics do, as evidence that even an apostle could fall away, and see in it a standing argument against unconditional security. On the crown, Protestants broadly resist the language of merit, preferring to say that God graciously rewards works He Himself produces, so that the reward is real but never earned. Both traditions agree that the warning is addressed to believers, that it is meant to be taken seriously rather than explained away, and that Christian life is a disciplined race with an outcome that matters.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
